newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels ready to make "ultimate sacrifice".
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels ready to make "ultimate sacrifice".

text.p: Peruvian guerrillas holding 83 VIP hostages inside the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima said on Tuesday they were "determined to make the ultimate sacrifice" in the two-week-old hostage crisis.
They also allowed a small group of journalists to approcah the building to hear the statement and then to enter the building.
The statement was shouted by an unidentified Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebel.

In a speech laced with revolutionary rhetoric and deliberately staged for maximum publicity, the rebel denied the MRTA was a terrorist group. He also slammed President Alberto Fujimori's government as a "dictatorship" that did not care about poverty.
"Peru is not a democracy. It is a dictatorship dressed up as a democracy," the rebel said from behind a window. "There is state terrorism that kills through starvation."

Reuters photographer Zoraida Diaz, among the first group of journalists to enter the building, said that furniture was pushed up against walls, barricading the windows. "Any object you can see has been pushed against the walls or put up against the windows," she said.

Hostages, including Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela -- the rebels' key hostage -- and Peruvian government legislator Gilberto Siura, were seen waving at journalists outside from the residence windows.

The MRTA's statement was its first public communication since a softer-worded communique was issued with 20 hostages released on Saturday night. The rebels were still holding 83 hostages on the 14th day of the crisis.

"Any harm to them (the hostages) will be the exclusive responsibility of the government of Fujimori if he decides upon a military intervention," the rebel added on Tuesday. He said that during Fujimori's time in office conditions in Peru's prisons had meant "the death penalty was applied in a slow fashion."
The MRTA's principal demand since storming the residence has been the release of around 400 jailed comrades. "We repeat that our prisoners should be freed," the rebel said.
The tone of the speech contrasted sharply with the new conciliatory mood struck since the weekend release and the preceding first face-to-face meeting between the guerrillas and the government.
Following a second surprise visit to the siege site late on Monday by government negotiator Domingo Palermo, hopes had been high of further releases on Tuesday.

Amid chaotic activity around the residence, police allowed journalists to approach the building in small groups from around 10:30 a.m. local time (1530 GMT). One group went into the building at about 11 a.m. local time (1600 GMT).

It was the first day journalists had been allowed to approach the front of the building -- with the exception of one cameraman who helped Red Cross officials take in supplies on the first days of the siege -- since the crisis began two weeks ago.

As the journalists were allowed to the front of the residence, television images of this side of the building transmitted for the first time showed it to be in almost the same condition as before the attack.
Vehicles of neighbours and guests at the cocktail party were still parked outside.
The Red Cross said in a statement the entry of the journalists was arranged between the Peruvian government and the MRTA.
